capabilities.target: Chat client of the authenticated requester
Jira tickets, including tickets filed by customers

inputs.source: Engineering design docs (confidential; write restricted to engineers)
Public web pages fetched by the planned web.fetch tool
Jira tickets filed by customers, via the planned Jira MCP server

instructions.note: The only control against leaking secrets or credentials found in design docs is a prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'). No structural redaction or output filter backs it.

The agent answers engineering questions for any SSO-authenticated employee, but the design docs are confidential and only engineers are stated to have write access. No per-requester authorization check is described for read/disclosure, so a non-engineer asking a question could receive confidential content via the agent that they could not access directly.

elements.name: Chat client of the authenticated requester
Planned Jira MCP server (includes customer-filed tickets)

controls.name: Read-only credential scope for docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the identity/platform layer, not the model. It blocks write or delete amplification but does not block disclosure of content the credential can read, so it narrows rather than severs.

controls.name: No network egress capability exists today
controls.decay_rationale: There is no tool today that can move data to an attacker-reachable external destination; this is an architectural absence rather than a configurable guardrail, so it fully blocks external exfiltration today. It ceases to exist the moment web.fetch ships (new_tool), which is exactly the condition this assessment forecasts.

controls.name: Reply destination bound to the authenticated requester
controls.decay_rationale: The recipient of cap.chat_reply comes from the authenticated session, not from model-chosen input, so a hijacked model cannot redirect the reply to a third party. It does not address disclosure to the requester themselves if they lack authorization for the specific content.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Removes a classic client-side side-channel egress vector (auto-fetched images/links in markdown), independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never paste secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply. A more capable or manipulated model can rationalize an exception or paraphrase/encode the secret to avoid a verbatim paste.

controls.name: Structural secret/credential redaction or DLP filter on chat_reply output
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. The only current control against leaking secrets is the behavioral prompt instruction, which decays with model capability.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for the planned web.fetch tool
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed. Without it, web.fetch can be directed to any destination, including one chosen to receive confidential data encoded in a query string, the moment the tool ships.

controls.name: Provenance tagging / spotlighting for Jira ticket and fetched web content
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed. Even implemented as a structural provenance tag, a sufficiently capable model can still act on untrusted instructions through legitimate-looking reasoning, so this would only partially resist capability growth.

controls.name: Action logging / audit trail for docs_search, chat_reply, and future web.fetch and jira.search calls
controls.decay_rationale: Not declared in the artifacts. Without it, neither the present baseline path nor the forecasted lethal-trifecta path would be detectable after the fact.

findings.title: Baseline Q&A path: confidential design-doc content reaches the chat reply

attack_path.note: Authenticated employee asks an engineering question
Agent includes doc content in its reply to the asking employee

forecast.watch_signal: Model version/id change in config, or a guardrail config change disabling destination binding or link/image rendering restrictions. The tier does not change under these triggers because the independent structural narrowing controls (destination binding, no-render client) already floor this path at low on their own.

evidence.observation: Replies go only to the authenticated requester; the chat client does not render images or fetch links; there is no network egress today; the credential is read only.
The agent answers engineering questions using docs.search and is told to cite sources and never paste secrets, with no structural DLP or per-document authorization check described.

recommendations.action: Add a structural secret/credential redaction or DLP check on chat_reply output instead of relying solely on the prompt instruction.
Confirm or add a per-document authorization check so a non-engineer requester cannot receive confidential design-doc content they are not cleared to see.
Add action logging/audit trail covering docs_search and chat_reply now, before adding new tools, to establish a baseline for anomaly detection.

findings.title: Forecast: lethal trifecta (TC1) via planned web.fetch and planned Jira MCP server

attack_path.note: Malicious instructions embedded in a customer-filed Jira ticket (planned)
Agent ingests ticket content while answering a related question (planned)
Following the injected instruction, the agent reads confidential design-doc content
Agent fetches an attacker-chosen URL with the confidential content encoded in the query string, exfiltrating it (planned)

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest diff adding web.fetch; MCP client config diff adding a Jira server; customer-ticket content appearing in agent context. Residual sits at high rather than critical only because the read-only credential scoping on docs_search still holds once these land; if that scope is also widened (data_scope_expansion) or the scoping is disabled (control_removal), projected risk rises to critical.

evidence.observation: Roadmap for next sprint: add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers. Neither is built yet.

Customer-filed tickets are authored by an external party (untrusted), and web.fetch lets the agent choose arbitrary destination URLs, which combined with a confidential-doc read in the same task matches the lethal-trifecta pattern.

recommendations.action: Before shipping web.fetch, add an egress allowlist that excludes attacker-writable or arbitrary destinations, and validate/strip query parameters so confidential content read earlier in the session cannot be encoded into outbound URLs.

Tag content ingested from the planned Jira MCP server (customer-filed tickets) as untrusted at the data layer, and require a human confirmation step before untrusted content can trigger new tool calls such as docs_search or web.fetch.
Add logging/anomaly detection that flags any session where a confidential-doc read and an outbound web.fetch call occur together, ahead of the Jira/web.fetch rollout.
Treat enabling web.fetch or the Jira MCP server as a significant change requiring reassessment before launch (ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.2), since both are the forecast triggers identified here.

rating.rationale: Today the agent is tightly scoped: a trusted, SSO-authenticated employee asks engineering questions, the agent reads confidential design docs with a read-only credential, and the only outbound path is a reply bound to the requester's own authenticated session, with no network egress tool and no link/image rendering. That keeps present-day residual risk at low. The roadmap, however, adds two things in the same sprint: a web.fetch tool (a new, model-chosen egress channel including the classic query-string exfiltration pattern) and a Jira MCP server whose content includes customer-filed tickets (an untrusted, U-class input). Once both land, the untrusted ticket content can drive the agent through the still-present confidential docs_search and into the new web.fetch egress channel, reconstructing the lethal-trifecta pattern (TC1) at a critical inherent level, held to high residual only by the pre-existing read-only credential scope on docs_search. No structural containment is yet planned for web.fetch or for treating Jira content as untrusted, so forecast risk is high and should be reassessed before either capability ships.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no tool manifest, MCP config, or IaC was provided.

Autonomy limits (max_unattended_steps, max_runtime_minutes) were not stated and were inferred as a narrow, single-turn search-then-reply pattern consistent with the described use case; confidence on this inference is medium.

The planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are described only at a one-line roadmap level with no scoping, auth method, or egress controls specified; the forecast finding uses conservative, generic assumptions about their sensitivity and reach, so confidence is medium and the finding should be revisited once a concrete design exists.

Whether employees other than engineers can ask questions that surface confidential design-doc content, and whether any per-user authorization check exists, is not stated; this is flagged as an instructions-level gap rather than a separate quantified finding.
